summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Vigil v. Division of Child & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the adjudication of domestic violence allegations because DCFS never gave Vigil notice that those allegations would be tried, while affirming the remaining rulings, including the standard of proof applied.
key_cases.relevance: The petition defines the scope of the adjudication; allegations outside it cannot be adjudicated.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the juvenile court erred by adjudicating the domestic violence allegations against Vigil because DCFS failed to provide Vigil proper notice

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the court of appeals' reversal of a neglect adjudication, holding that nondeferential review was appropriate for the law-like mixed question and that the juvenile court's findings did not satisfy the statutory definition of neglect (or of abuse as an alternative ground).
key_cases.relevance: A petition must plead and prove facts that fit the statutory grounds, or the adjudication cannot stand.
key_cases.quote: the juvenile court's factual findings do not support any of the statutory grounds for neglect

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that the mother had been advised of and validly waived her statutory right to counsel at the adjudication hearing, that the unappealed adjudication order was separately final, and that denial of a merely statutory right to counsel requires a showing of prejudice.
key_cases.relevance: It establishes that the adjudication order opening a dependency case is separately final and appealable, and that the right to counsel there is statutory rather than constitutional.
key_cases.quote: because the right to counsel in child welfare proceedings is a statutory right, prejudice must be shown

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that there is no automatic federal constitutional right to appointed counsel in parental termination proceedings; the presumption is against appointment absent a risk of loss of physical liberty, and the question is decided case by case under Mathews v. Eldridge.
key_cases.relevance: It explains why the right to counsel for Utah parents when a petition is filed rests on statute (Utah Code § 80-3-104) rather than on the federal Constitution.
key_cases.quote: right to appointed counsel only when, if he loses, he may be deprived of his physical liberty

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that the stepfather was not denied due process where he participated through counsel in both the shelter and adjudication hearings, and that the juvenile court could properly rely at adjudication on evidence presented during the seven-day shelter hearing given the parties' agreement.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses the procedural relationship between the shelter hearing and the adjudication on the petition.
key_cases.quote: we presume that those findings are supported by the evidence presented during the seven-day shelter hearing

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that a mother's fundamental parental rights were severed when the district court terminated them for failing to strictly comply with the Adoption Act's intervention procedures, and that the strict-compliance provision of Utah Code section 78B-6-110 failed strict scrutiny and was unconstitutional as applied to her because her timely, substantially compliant motion achieved everything the provision exists to achieve.
key_cases.relevance: It is the modern Utah Supreme Court authority on what process is due a parent at the pleading stage: a procedural default rule may not be applied to sever parental rights unless doing so actually serves a compelling state interest.
key_cases.quote: because the strict compliance requirement did not further the State's compelling, adoption-related interests in this case, we hold that the strict compliance requirement is unconstitutional as applied in this case
